title: Given a set of distinct positive numbers and a target, find all unique combinations that sum to the target, where each number may be reused unlimited times.

s1_definition.profdef: Combination Sum asks for every multiset of numbers, drawn from a given set and allowing repeats, whose total equals a target. Backtracking solves it by choosing numbers from a start index onward, subtracting each choice from a remaining target, and recursing; when the remaining target hits zero you record the combination, and when it goes negative you prune that branch. Reusing the same start index on recursion is what permits unlimited reuse of a number.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India must make up an exact payout amount using denominations it can dispense in unlimited quantity, and it wants every distinct way to hit that amount. A clerk picks a denomination, sets aside that much from the target, and keeps picking, allowed to pick the same denomination again. If she reaches exactly zero she has found one valid way; if she overshoots she abandons that attempt and backs up. To avoid listing the same combination in different orders, she never goes back to a smaller denomination once she has moved past it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Subtract a chosen number from the remaining target and recurse from the same index for reuse; record at zero, prune below zero.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Combination Sum asks for every multiset of numbers, drawn from a given set and allowing repeats, whose total equals a target. Backtracking solves it by choosing numbers from a start index onward, subtracting each choice from a remaining target, and recursing; when the remaining target hits zero you record the combination, and when it goes negative you prune that branch. Reusing the same start index on recursion is what permits unlimited reuse of a number.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India must make up an exact payout amount using denominations it can dispense in unlimited quantity, and it wants every distinct way to hit that amount. A clerk picks a denomination, sets aside that much from the target, and keeps picking, allowed to pick the same denomination again. If she reaches exactly zero she has found one valid way; if she overshoots she abandons that attempt and backs up. To avoid listing the same combination in different orders, she never goes back to a smaller denomination once she has moved past it.

**One line to remember:** Subtract a chosen number from the remaining target and recurse from the same index for reuse; record at zero, prune below zero.

sections.s2_technical:
This is a backtracking search over a decision tree where the state is the remaining target and the index you are allowed to start choosing from. The twin base cases drive everything: if the remaining target is exactly zero you have a complete combination and record a copy of the running path, and if the remaining target is negative you return immediately because adding more positive numbers can never come back to zero. That negative-target pruning is what keeps the search finite and efficient.

The loop runs from a start index over the candidates. For each candidate you add it to the path and recurse, but the crucial detail is the index you pass. To allow reusing the same number, you recurse with the same index i, not i plus one: `backtrack(candidates, remaining - candidates[i], i, path, result);`. Passing i again means the next level may pick the same candidate; passing i plus one would forbid reuse, which is the variant for combinations without repetition. After recursing you remove the last element to backtrack.

Starting each loop at the current index rather than zero is what prevents duplicate combinations that differ only in order, for example two-then-three versus three-then-two; by never looking back at earlier candidates you fix a non-decreasing order and so each distinct multiset is produced once. Sorting the candidates first lets you add an even stronger prune: once a candidate exceeds the remaining target, every later candidate does too, so you can break out of the loop entirely.

A senior-level nuance is the complexity, which is exponential in the worst case because the number of valid combinations can itself be large, bounded by the target divided by the smallest candidate as the maximum depth. For money I use BigDecimal, subtracting with `subtract` and comparing against zero with `compareTo`. The same template, with small tweaks to the index and a duplicate-skip, solves Combination Sum without reuse and with duplicate candidates, which is why this is a cornerstone backtracking pattern.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's cash-dispensing module must enumerate every way to make up an exact withdrawal amount from available note denominations, each dispensable in unlimited quantity, so an optimiser can later pick the best mix. This is exactly Combination Sum with reuse.

Problem 2 — Each distinct mix must appear once regardless of the order notes are chosen, and overshooting the amount must be abandoned immediately rather than explored further. The start-index discipline removes order-duplicates and the negative-remaining prune stops wasteful branches.

In our mini-project we build a `NoteCombiner` that returns all combinations of denominations summing to a target using backtracking. The demo targets a small amount with a few denominations and logs each combination.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: denominations two, three, five sorted, and a target of eight.

Step 1: Enter backtrack with remaining eight, start zero, empty path. Loop from index zero. Pick two, remaining becomes six, recurse with the same index zero so two can repeat.

Step 2: With remaining six, pick two again, remaining four, recurse. Pick two again, remaining two, recurse. Pick two again, remaining zero, record two, two, two, two. Backtrack.

Step 3: At remaining two with start zero, try three, which exceeds two, so by the sorted break we stop that loop. Backtrack up the chain of twos.

Step 4: At remaining four with twos chosen, move to three, remaining one, recurse, nothing fits one so no record, backtrack. The branch of three twos did not reach zero cleanly beyond what was found.

Step 5: Exploring picks that start with two then three: two, three, three gives eight, recorded. Exploring two then five: two plus five is seven, then nothing sums the last one, but three plus five is eight when starting with three: three, five recorded.

Step 6: After all branches, the valid combinations summing to eight are two-two-two-two, two-three-three, and three-five. Each is produced once because the start index keeps picks non-decreasing, and overshoot branches were pruned immediately.

```
[2026-10-26 23:34:01] INFO    Ways to make 8: 3
[2026-10-26 23:34:01] INFO      combo: [2, 2, 2, 2]
[2026-10-26 23:34:01] INFO      combo: [2, 3, 3]
[2026-10-26 23:34:01] INFO      combo: [3, 5]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  candidates (sorted): [2,3,5]   target=8

  rem8 ─2→ rem6 ─2→ rem4 ─2→ rem2 ─2→ rem0 [2,2,2,2]
                          └3→ rem1
             └3→ rem3 ─3→ rem0 [2,3,3]
  rem8 ─3→ rem5 ─5→ rem0 [3,5]
  rem8 ─5→ rem3 ─ (only ≥5 left, break)

  record at rem==0; break when candidate > rem (sorted)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Combination Sum (Backtracking) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Backtracking with remaining-target + start index            │
  │  Reuse via same-index recursion; sorted early-break prune    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: NoteCombiner only enumerates summing combinations         │
  │  O: pass i+1 instead of i for no-reuse variant                │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             NoteCombiner              │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + combinations(cands[], target): List│  exponential worst case
  │  - backtrack(cands, rem, start, p, r) │  record at 0, prune <0
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Pre:  candidates distinct positive
      Post: all unique multisets summing to target

  ── State Diagram: Remaining target ──────────────────────

  [rem > 0] ──pick c ≤ rem──→ rem-c, recurse(same i)
  [rem == 0] ──→ record combination
  [c > rem, sorted] ──→ break (prune)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. combinations → sort → backtrack(target, 0, [])
  2.   rem==0 → record copy
  3.   for i=start: if c>rem break; add; recurse(rem-c, i); remove
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Combination Sum asks for every combination of numbers from a given set, allowing each number to be reused any number of times, that adds up to a target. I solve it with backtracking over a decision tree whose state is the remaining target and the index I am allowed to start choosing from. There are two base cases that drive the whole search: if the remaining target reaches exactly zero I have a valid combination and record a copy, and if it goes negative I abandon the branch immediately because adding more positive numbers can never return to zero.

The loop runs from a start index over the candidates, and for each candidate I add it to the path and recurse. The one detail that defines this problem is the index I pass on recursion: to allow reusing the same number I recurse with the same index, not the next one, so the next level is free to pick the same candidate again. Starting each loop at the current index rather than zero is what stops me generating the same combination in different orders, because it fixes a non-decreasing order, so each distinct multiset appears exactly once. If I sort the candidates first, I gain a strong prune: once a candidate exceeds the remaining target, so does every later one, so I can break the loop entirely.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the cash-dispensing module to enumerate every way to make up an exact withdrawal amount from note denominations that can be dispensed in unlimited quantity, feeding the list to an optimiser that later chooses the best mix. The start-index discipline removed order-duplicates and the negative-remaining prune stopped wasteful exploration.

The senior-level point I make is that this is a cornerstone backtracking template with exponential worst-case cost, because the number of valid combinations itself can be large, and I state that honestly. The same skeleton solves the neighbouring problems with tiny changes: passing the next index instead of the same one gives combinations without reuse, and adding a skip of equal consecutive candidates handles inputs with duplicates, so once I have this pattern I have the whole family.
